title: Introducing OpenDocRouter: Call any OCR model in a single line of code
summary: OpenDocRouter turns PDFs and images into clean markdown using the latest frontier and open-source OCR models, including Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 3.8 Flash, GPT-6 Luna, MinerU2.5-Pro and PaddleOCR-VL. Switching models means changing one parameter. You don't touch prompts, rate limits or deployments. Every model is benchmarked on ParseBench for both quality and cost. Turn on layout and any model returns grounded bounding boxes with the same set of layout classes, even models that can't do this natively. Billing is pay-per-token, starting as low as $0.80 per 1,000 pages, and you aren't charged for pages that fail. ▶ Try it: https://www.opendocrouter.ai/ ▶ Docs: https://www.opendocrouter.ai/docs ▶ Models + benchmarks: https://www.opendocrouter.ai/models ▶ Launch blog: https://www.llamaindex.ai/blog/introducing-opendocrouter

title: Stop Brain Drain: The Strategy to Build Deep Tech in India
summary: While Indian academic institutions generate world-class deep-tech research, translating lab-stage innovations into viable, commercialized market products remains a key hurdle. Established under the Department of Science and Technology (DST), Government of India, Technology Innovation Hubs (TIHs) at premier institutes like IIT Bombay bridge this gap by funding seed-stage startups, advancing physical AI systems, and converting academic intellectual property into industry-ready solutions. In this interview recorded live at Cypher 2026, Sudhi Sachdev speaks with Dhruti Pillai, Assistant Vice President (AVP) of Technology at TIH, IIT Bombay. They explore reversing the traditional tech "brain drain" in favor of indigenous innovation, funding early-stage founders in physical AI, navigating enterprise procurement and corporate adoption risks, balancing ground-level reality with government policy, and leveraging frugal innovation to build sovereign technology capabilities for India. title: Prompt Regression Tester
summary: Compares a trusted prompt with a proposed change over the same test suite, three runs per case, and calls a regression only when the baseline holds and the candidate keeps failing. By Benjamin Nweke Project page: https://towardsdatascience.com/shipai/projects/prompt-regression-tester ShipAI is a Towards Data Science project. You can learn more about it here: https://towardsdatascience.com/shipai/about Key takeaways. 1. Each case runs three times per prompt, so a regression means a stable baseline pass and a stable candidate fail. 2. Hard checks guard dates, numbers and review states; an LLM judge with a rubric scores meaning, and disagreements stay visible. 3. On an EvidenceDesk suite, a candidate that swapped dates for “earlier” and “later” failed the versioned case 3 of 3. Chapters: 0:00 Why prompt changes deceive 0:52 An EvidenceDesk-style suite 2:07 Baseline versus candidate 3:16 Repeated runs and split checks 4:42 Under the hood 5:25 One confirmed regression 6:19 When dates are evidence 8:10 When the judge disagrees

title: Autonomous MCP Agent
summary: An agent that finds open-source MCP servers on GitHub at run time, runs them in throwaway uvx environments, and replans when a tool fails. By Partha Sarkar Project page: https://towardsdatascience.com/shipai/projects/auto-mcp ShipAI is a Towards Data Science project. You can learn more about it here: https://towardsdatascience.com/shipai/about Key takeaways. 1. A planner splits the task, a discovery agent finds MCP servers on GitHub, and uvx runs each in isolation. 2. When the SQLite insert failed on a missing table, the LangGraph supervisor replanned: create the table first, then retry. 3. Three finance servers failed the stock briefing; a whitelisted yfinance-mcp fixed it, and working tools get reused for later steps. Chapters: 0:00 Why fixed tool sets 0:51 Planning a trip across India 2:58 Stock briefing: three servers fail 4:35 Whitelisting yfinance-mcp 5:15 Self-healing a SQLite insert 8:07 The agent pipeline

title: Mistral Large 4 aka "le Chonk": Europe's Biggest Open Model
summary: Mistral just announced Mistral Large 4, officially nicknamed "le Chonk." It's a mixture-of-experts model with about 1 trillion total parameters and around 50 billion active per token. It takes text and images and has a 1 million token context window. Mistral says it's a frontier-level open-weight model: competitive with the strongest open models in the world, and well ahead of any open model built in the US or Europe, especially on coding agents, cybersecurity, finance, and law. All benchmark numbers here are Mistral's own; independent results aren't in yet. Right now it's a preview API. Mistral says the open weights land at the end of October. Sources: Mistral announcement: https://mistral.ai/news/mistral-large-4/ Model docs: https://docs.mistral.ai/models/mistral-large-4-0 CNBC: https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/06/mistral-ai-model-le-chonk.html #MistralAI #MistralLarge4 #OpenSourceAI #LLM #AI #shorts

title: How Spec-Driven Development Reduces Context Debt
summary: As AI-assisted projects grow, important decisions can get buried in chat histories, scattered prompts, and undocumented assumptions. How do you keep that context from getting lost? Hari Krishnan, author of Spec-Driven Development, discusses how spec-driven development helps reduce context debt by making intent explicit and keeping specifications relevant as software evolves. title: Cleveland Clinic, RIKEN, and IBM simulate 12,635-atom protein complex
summary: It can take more than a decade for a medical discovery to become a drug doctors can prescribe. Researchers from @Cleveland Clinic, RIKEN and IBM are exploring how hybrid quantum-classical workflows could help accelerate this timeline–with exciting results. Earlier this year, the collaboration successfully simulated the chemistry of two protein complexes with binding agents, T4-Lysozyme and Trypsin. The largest simulation of a Trypsin complex reached 12,635 atoms and more than 30,000 orbitals, earning the milestone of largest heterogeneous quantum-classical (HQC) electronic-structure calculation to date: https://www.ibm.com/quantum/blog/cleveland-clinic-riken-chemistry Recently nominated as a 2026 Gordon Bell finalist (https://www.ibm.com/quantum/blog/gordon-bell-finalists-2026), the work showed an improvement in accuracy by 210x within a key step of the workflow over previous approaches, attained through new algorithm developments and the close integration of QPUs, CPUs and GPUs. In the latest entry of our research spotlight series, Dr. Kennie Merz. and Dr. Lara Jehi from Cleveland Clinic join IBM Quantum Head of Applied Quantum Science - Sarah Sheldon to explain how this deep integration of computing paradigms, known as quantum-centric supercomputing, helped achieve this remarkable moment in chemistry simulation at scale.

title: Jev AI vs Open Source: Can GLiNER Replace It?
summary: Jev is one of the most hyped AI models of the year, and it isn't an LLM. TypeSafe's "System One" model doesn't generate text. It makes typed, calibrated decisions in ~90ms. In this video we cover what Jev is and how its API works. We look at why calibrated probability is the real unlock, where Jev fits next to LLMs (and where it doesn't), and the open-source "OpenJev" alternatives you can run on your own machine. Finally, we think fast and slow, pairing a System One model with an LLM coach to beat solo Jev at Doom. 📌 Full article with benchmarks, charts and methodology: https://jamesbriggs.io/understanding-jev What we found: - Calibration: Jev's confidence means something. ECE 0.053 vs 0.119 for gpt-5.6-luna on CLINC150. - Speed: ~90ms per call on the server vs ~700ms for gpt-5.6-luna with no reasoning. Extra questions in the same call add no latency. - Accuracy: Jev matches or beats gpt-5.6-luna on 5 of 6 intent, tool-selection and guardrail benchmarks. - Open source: GLiNER2.5 and GLiGuard run in 10–50ms on an M4 Pro Mac and come close on several benchmarks. They don't match Jev's calibration yet. - Fast + slow: adding an LLM coach to Jev and GLiNER gives ~4x their solo Doom deathmatch scores. ⏱️ Chapters 0:00 Intro 1:22 What is JEV? 2:40 Inputs and outputs 4:26 Three types of decision 6:35 Calibrated probability 10:38 Ultra-fast 11:44 Where JEV fits 14:58 Closed source 16:39 Open-source alternatives 20:28 GLiNER 23:33 The trade-offs 25:42 Thinking fast and slow 31:30 What to make of JEV 👋 Find me X: https://x.com/jamescalam LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/jamescalam/ GitHub: https://github.com/jamescalam #AI #LLM #AIAgents
summary_html:
Jev is one of the most hyped AI models of the year, and it isn't an LLM. TypeSafe's "System One" model doesn't generate text. It makes typed, calibrated decisions in ~90ms.

In this video we cover what Jev is and how its API works. We look at why calibrated probability is the real unlock, where Jev fits next to LLMs (and where it doesn't), and the open-source "OpenJev" alternatives you can run on your own machine. Finally, we think fast and slow, pairing a System One model with an LLM coach to beat solo Jev at Doom.

📌 Full article with benchmarks, charts and methodology:
https://jamesbriggs.io/understanding-jev

What we found:
- Calibration: Jev's confidence means something. ECE 0.053 vs 0.119 for gpt-5.6-luna on CLINC150.
- Speed: ~90ms per call on the server vs ~700ms for gpt-5.6-luna with no reasoning. Extra questions in the same call add no latency.
- Accuracy: Jev matches or beats gpt-5.6-luna on 5 of 6 intent, tool-selection and guardrail benchmarks.
- Open source: GLiNER2.5 and GLiGuard run in 10–50ms on an M4 Pro Mac and come close on several benchmarks. They don't match Jev's calibration yet.
- Fast + slow: adding an LLM coach to Jev and GLiNER gives ~4x their solo Doom deathmatch scores.

title: Context Language Models Explained!
summary: Context management is one of the biggest bottlenecks for AI agents. When the context window fills up, most harnesses compact or summarize the conversation and lose useful information along the way. Meta and the University of Washington's new paper, Context Language Models, lets the agent edit its own context like a file instead. The catch: it breaks your prefix caching. title: Grounded Generation, Hallucinations & LLM Evaluation: Assessing Model Output Quality
summary: AI can be confidently wrong. Here is why it happens, how grounding fixes it, and how to measure whether it worked. Terms covered: - Hallucination: models are trained to generate statistically likely text, not to verify facts. When a model does not know, it fills the gap with something plausible. - Grounded Generation: anchoring responses in verified, retrieved sources so answers are traceable and far less likely to be fabricated - LLM Evaluation: assessing outputs for accuracy, relevance, coherence, cost and safety, as an ongoing practice rather than a one-time check - RAG Evaluation: measuring retrieval and generation separately, because a system can retrieve well and generate poorly, or generate fluently from the wrong sources The goal is not perfect AI. It is trustworthy AI, and that requires knowing how to measure it. — AI Fundamentals Glossary | H2O.ai University Full playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLAWKlIKS-66E Free courses and certifications: https://h2o.ai/university #LLM #Hallucinations #ResponsibleAI #AIGlossary #H2Oai
summary_html:
AI can be confidently wrong. Here is why it happens, how grounding fixes it, and how to measure whether it worked.

Terms covered:
- Hallucination: models are trained to generate statistically likely text, not to verify facts. When a model does not know, it fills the gap with something plausible.
- Grounded Generation: anchoring responses in verified, retrieved sources so answers are traceable and far less likely to be fabricated
- LLM Evaluation: assessing outputs for accuracy, relevance, coherence, cost and safety, as an ongoing practice rather than a one-time check
- RAG Evaluation: measuring retrieval and generation separately, because a system can retrieve well and generate poorly, or generate fluently from the wrong sources

The goal is not perfect AI. It is trustworthy AI, and that requires knowing how to measure it.

—

title: How a Logistics Giant Keeps AI Data Locked Down
summary: Picture a startup with ten engineers hammering away on AI and one person lying awake over a $20,000 bill that hasn't arrived yet. That's the scenario we put to Jason Ward, who handles FinOps for AI at C.H. Robinson and recently joined the FinOps Foundation's AI working group. Jason's first answer is not glamorous: tag every AI resource so you know who owns it. The rest of the episode is what that makes possible. He walks through how C.H. Robinson runs AI across order entry, quoting, booking, and tracking, and why the team routes Anthropic models through Vertex AI to keep data locked down. Then come the metrics. Jason uses AI to dig through his own observability platform for signals he didn't know were there. One of them is how chatty a model is. That signal turned a prompt bloat alert into a bug in the code that kept retrying and burning tokens. Its opposite, context starvation, burns tokens too: a model with too little context keeps failing and trying again. We also cover why agentic and conversational workloads need separate baselines. Jason explains why cost per order is the easy win, and why most of the real work doesn't fit into neat discrete tasks. That's where his experimental cost per thought metric comes in, with reasoning ratio and cache hit rate alongside it. His advice is simple: your AI is the best tool you have for understanding your AI. title: Specification vs. Prompt: What’s the Difference?
summary: A detailed prompt can help an AI coding agent complete a task—but a specification does much more. It captures the durable intent behind a project, including its goals, requirements, constraints, expected behaviors, and success criteria. Hari Krishnan, author of Spec-Driven Development, explains why specifications provide a shared source of truth that teams can review, refine, test, and maintain as software evolves—rather than temporary instructions for a single AI interaction. title: Stanford Univ: New AI Attention: SwiLA
summary: Softmax attention’s KV-cache is a dead end for infinite (or extreme large) context, but standard Linear Attention fundamentally destroys associative recall (Mamba, DeltaNet). So how do we get the best of both worlds? Meet SwiLA (Switching Linear Attention) by Stanford Univ. Switching Linear Attention completely eliminates the transformer's massive memory cache without sacrificing associative recall by modeling sequence routing as online expectation-maximization over a mixture of linear regressors. Dive into the math of how this non-linear recurrence dynamically routes context to constant-size memory experts, finally fixing the critical flaw of sub-quadratic language models. All rights w/ authors: Switching Linear Attention Hyun Dong Lee∗ Stanford University Xavier Gonzalez Stanford University† Nicolas Zucchet Stanford University E. Kelly Buchanan Stanford University Emily B. Fox Stanford University Scott W. Linderman Stanford University arXiv:2609.39034 #airesearch #aitechnology #aiexplained #newstoday

title: How Salesforce Untangled Its Own Data Chaos
summary: In episode 1032 of the SuperDataScience podcast, Jon Krohn discusses with Michael Andrew, CDO at Salesforce how Salesforce tackled its internal data chaos, including duplicate records and disparate systems, leading to the development and deployment of their Data 360 product. Michael explains how they unified customer data from various sources like Snowflake, Amazon data lake, and multiple Salesforce instances to create a single, actionable customer view. This integration now allows their sales team to receive proactive alerts, such as when a customer is about to run out of credits, demonstrating the power of a connected data strategy.

title: How Many Iterations Does a Good Spec Need?
summary: A strong specification rarely emerges fully formed. It improves through focused iteration—clarifying assumptions, resolving ambiguity, testing edge cases, and aligning the intended outcome with real constraints. Hari Krishnan, author of Spec-Driven Development, explains how teams can refine a specification and why there’s no universal number of iterations. The goal isn’t perfection—it’s reaching the point where developers and AI coding agents have enough shared context to implement the right solution confidently. title: SLMs, Fine-Tuning & LLMOps: Building Production-Ready Language Models
summary: Not every use case needs a large model. Smaller and purpose-built is often faster, cheaper and better suited to the job. Terms covered: - SLM (Small Language Model): fewer parameters, trading breadth for precision. Runs on-premises or on edge devices with no cloud dependency. - SLM Development: designing, training and optimizing a small model for a well-defined task or dataset - Fine-Tuning Engine: taking a pre-trained model and training it further on domain-specific data, so it learns the language of law, medicine or your business - LLMOps: the infrastructure and practices for deploying, managing, monitoring and updating language models over time A hospital running clinical documentation on local servers. A manufacturer processing quality reports on factory floor devices. These are where compact models win. — AI Fundamentals Glossary | H2O.ai University Full playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLAWKlIKS-66E Free courses and certifications: https://h2o.ai/university #SLM #FineTuning #LLMOps #AIGlossary #H2Oai

title: How a Voice Agent Learns the Rhythm of Conversation — Shawn Wen
summary: Tsung-Hsien (Shawn) Wen, CTO of PolyAI, tells Tim Scarfe why voice agents are harder than text agents. Voice adds time, and a good conversation depends on adapting to the person on the line, not just on reasoning to the best answer. Shawn describes an audio-native model (Dialog-RSN-1) that first predicts a turn-taking signal, then replies in text with citations, and writes the transcript last so enterprises can audit it. Along the way: training on real, noisy calls with synthetic noise added, and why over-cleaned audio made the new model worse. Latency, and what a voice agent should do while it thinks. Why a voice with a hint of regional accent beats a generic one. Why public benchmarks fall short for voice, why enterprises want to own their agent harness, and whether behaviour belongs in the harness or in the weights. The last stretch is about working with agents: cognitive debt, the shift from producing content to checking it, Wispr Flow, building tools that agents can use, and whether slop is in the eye of the reader. This episode was produced in partnership with PolyAI. https://poly.ai CHAPTERS 0:00 Why voice agents are harder than text 4:27 What enterprises want, and why PolyAI built its own model 9:04 How an audio-native voice model works 15:21 Training data, spectrograms and synthetic noise 20:36 The cocktail party problem and the future of turn-taking 25:21 Latency, adaptive reasoning and keeping callers' trust 31:33 Voices, personality and the uncanny valley 36:32 How do you benchmark a voice agent? 42:00 Harness engineering and owning the intelligence 45:09 Well-specified problems and auditable agents 49:46 Weight adaptation and cognitive debt 56:31 Agents at work: Wispr Flow, voice and tool building 1:02:50 The next decade of voice, and what counts as slop REFERENCES The Bitter Lesson: http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html [9:05] Retrieval-augmented generation: https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401 [13:23] Mel scale: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel_scale [17:16] Victor Zue: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Zue [17:45] Cocktail party effect: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocktail_party_effect [20:39] Speaker diarisation: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_diarisation [21:16]

title: The Caveman Prompting Challenge
summary: Caveman prompting has one rule: why use many words when few do the trick? It saves tokens on the way in and on the way out. Push it too far, though, and the output falls apart. So how far is too far? Nobody has benchmarked it yet, and that question opens our conversation with James Barney, Head of Forward Labs at MetLife. James spends his days connecting new AI capabilities to old business problems across dozens of regulatory regimes, and he still finds time to push code. He explains how the FinOps Foundation's AI working group took on the most basic question: which model for which workload, and why the answer always comes down to cost, speed, and accuracy. We get into Anthropic's launch pricing for Fable, why a million tokens is easy to price and hard to explain, and why every stakeholder eventually tells you what they really care about once you name the wrong North Star. From there it gets practical. Start with the smartest model, then step down and add harness until quality holds. Treat exploration tokens like local builds and production tokens like pipelines. Govern agents the way you govern people, with proactive blocks, reactive checks, and policy as code an agent can actually read. We close on a bigger shift. When a chat window can pull from every dashboard at once, do we still need dashboards? James thinks mostly not, with one catch he calls the latent shopper problem: some insights only come from browsing data you did not know to ask about. summary_html:
Caveman prompting has one rule: why use many words when few do the trick? It saves tokens on the way in and on the way out. Push it too far, though, and the output falls apart. So how far is too far? Nobody has benchmarked it yet, and that question opens our conversation with James Barney, Head of Forward Labs at MetLife.

James spends his days connecting new AI capabilities to old business problems across dozens of regulatory regimes, and he still finds time to push code. He explains how the FinOps Foundation's AI working group took on the most basic question: which model for which workload, and why the answer always comes down to cost, speed, and accuracy. We get into Anthropic's launch pricing for Fable, why a million tokens is easy to price and hard to explain, and why every stakeholder eventually tells you what they really care about once you name the wrong North Star.

From there it gets practical. Start with the smartest model, then step down and add harness until quality holds. Treat exploration tokens like local builds and production tokens like pipelines. Govern agents the way you govern people, with proactive blocks, reactive checks, and policy as code an agent can actually read.

We close on a bigger shift. When a chat window can pull from every dashboard at once, do we still need dashboards? James thinks mostly not, with one catch he calls the latent shopper problem: some insights only come from browsing data you did not know to ask about.

title: Meet The Startup: Probabl: by the Creators of Scikit-Learn
summary: The creators of scikit-learn are GPU-accelerating machine learning — and partnering with NVIDIA to do it. Yann Lechelle, co-founder of Probabl, sat down with us to share why the team behind the world's most downloaded ML framework is doubling down on statistical machine learning — not generative AI — and what that means for the future of tabular data. Scikit-learn has surpassed 5 billion downloads, with 1.3 million GitHub projects depending on it. It's the backbone of data science as we know it. But it was built for CPUs — and the world has changed. Probabl is now offloading key algorithms to GPU, leveraging the Array API as an abstraction layer so that new generations of NVIDIA chips plug in seamlessly, without rewriting everything from scratch. Their new product, Skore, wraps scikit-learn and tabular large models into a unified ML platform — with the goal of becoming the world's leading tabular AI company within five years. And as Yann points out, it's not just data scientists using these tools anymore: agents are now the largest driver of scikit-learn downloads, consuming documentation and frameworks at machine speed. The partnership with NVIDIA Inception is about more than compute — it's about building the abstraction layer that maximizes intelligence per gigawatt, for humans and agents alike. Learn more about how NVIDIA Inception supports startups building the future of AI — and explore what GPU-accelerated ML can do for your workflows at nvidia.com/inception.

title: Gemini 4 Argon: The New Frontier
summary: Gemini 4 Argon can generate up to 1 million output tokens in a single response, up from 64K in earlier Gemini models. Most frontier models today cap a single response at around 128K. Arena's testing puts Argon on the Pareto frontier of performance vs. cost: 33% lower cost per task than GPT-6.1 Sol and 70% lower than Claude Opus 5.5. Argon isn't publicly available yet. It's rolling out first to trusted testers through Google's Fairwind program. Fun fact: argon is the third most abundant gas in Earth's atmosphere. Sources: Google announcement: https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/gemini-4-argon/ Arena's results: https://x.com/arena/status/2105449871671173257 #Gemini4 #GeminiArgon #GoogleDeepMind #AI #LLM #Shorts
